newsitem.title: SPAIN: BoS could wait before using scope to cut its rate.
newsitem.headline: BoS could wait before using scope to cut its rate.

text.p: Many economists believe the Bank of Spain has room to cut its official rate as soon as next week, but some believe the move would be risky in terms of inflation and general nervousness over the monetary union.

A Reuter poll conducted on Friday showed nine out of 16 analysts were in favour of a 25-basis-point cut as soon as next Tuesday, but the remaining seven suggested it would stay flat, saying the 18-month-old monetary easing cycle was losing fuel.
"I'll give 70 percent probability to a cut, but at the end whether it actually cuts or not does not matter so much," said Jose Ramon Arechederra, trader at ABN Amro in Madrid.

Spanish inflation hit a record low in May, with CPI rising 1.5 percent year on year versus 1.7 percent in April, and expectations of a pick-up in the second part of the year suggest that the time for an easing is running out quickly.
"After May CPI, I think that the Bank of Spain can cut by 25 basis points on Tuesday," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.

But signs of an economic recovery, together with possible tensions and jitters in the international markets due to uncertainty over the European economic and monetary union are suggesting a more prudent approach.
"I do not think this is the right time to cut the rate," said Elena Pagola, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacionales (AFI) in Madrid.

April industrial production, which rose 17.7 percent year on year versus a fall of 0.2 percent in March, and 4.2 percent rise in wage inflation in the first quarter, showed that economic growth was taking off.
Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told journalists following Friday's cabinet meeting that the government was worried that wage rises were outstripping inflation.
"The market is starting to think Spain is experiencing a mini-boom," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
But some analysts think the economy's revival should not inhibit the Bank of Spain from using the scope it has.
"I do not think the economy needs that (the cut), but the Bank of Spain has room to cut given better inflation," said William Thornill at Technical Data in London.
He said there is a 51 percent probability the bank will cut.
Others added that another monetary easing would not endanger the stability of the exchange rate.
"A 25-basis point cut will not threaten the peseta which has proved to be stable," said Valentin Fernandez, economist of Credit Lyonnais.
"This is the time for another cut, when inflation picks up that will be worse," he added.
